Subject: Re: On-prem provisioning questions for small-office deployment

Hi Markus,

Thanks again for taking a look at our site inventory (attached). A few constraints up front so you can tailor guidance: this is a single-rack, single-cage installation at our Raleigh office. Hardware we can commit right now: 3x GPU hosts (each 4x A100, local NVMe: 2 x 2TB per host) and a compact NAS appliance with 24TB usable (RAID6 presented over iSCSI). No dedicated storage fabric (no SAN switches) and limited rack PDUs (we want to avoid adding more heavy-power racks).

Primary goals: run Redwood Private for inference with predictable latency for inference endpoints and maintain model artifact durability and operator-friendly backups. We can't add more servers for a separate storage cluster, and our networking is a single top-of-rack switch with routed uplink to the customer DC; MTU is 1500.

Main asks:
- Recommended cluster footprint (control plane + worker mix) given our hardware constraint?
- How to layout node roles so inference nodes don't cause eviction of critical persistent volumes when we hit heavy write/IO on model cache?
- Approaches to ensure model artifacts are durable without a full-scale distributed storage cluster (our NAS is the only shared store).

I attached the inventory CSV and a quick diagram. If you can sketch a minimal topology and any runbook checks we should run before Go‑Live that would be great.

Evan
Site Reliability Lead, Nebula Health

Evan — thanks for the details and the inventory. High level — we can support a robust Private deployment in that footprint but we need to be explicit about a few tradeoffs since you can’t add hardware immediately. I sketched a minimal, resilient pattern below (attaching a short draft runbook).

Proposal (summary):
- Control-plane: 3 control-plane instances co-located on the existing hosts using small CPU reservations and static kubelet admission to avoid scheduler churn. Keep control-plane nodes non-schedulable for heavy inference pods (taints + tolerations).
- Worker split: reserve 2 GPU hosts primarily for inference workers, force-pinned with nodeSelector and kube-reserved resources. Keep the 3rd host as a mixed worker + local storage gateway host (see below) to reduce cross-node IO storm impact.
- Local NVMe use: use local NVMe on inference hosts for model KV cache and transient artifacts (hostPath via CSI-local or local persistent volumes with topology-aware provisioning). Keep aggressive eviction thresholds for cache TTL (use our agent to prune).
- Persistent artifacts: present the NAS over iSCSI to a small set of storage-gateway pods (run on the mixed host). Those pods export a read-only S3-like layer (minio in read-replica mode) for model artifacts and snapshotting. We will not run a full distributed block store; instead treat NAS as the single source of truth and keep copies of model shards on local NVMe for performance.
- IO containment: enable cgroups blkio throttling on inference pods and use Kubernetes QoS with PodOverhead to cap write bursts. Also configure kubelet eviction thresholds: nodefs.inodesFree, nodefs.available at conservative levels given a single-disk scenario.
- Networking: avoid MTU >1500 features; enable TCP BBR and tune conntrack for expected concurrency. Recommend a BGP or static route from the ToR to the DC only if you need cross-site fallback.

Risks and mitigations:
- Single NAS = single point of durability. Mitigation: nightly encrypted snapshots to a cloud object store (we can automate via a signed transfer job).
- Heavy model downloads on bootstrap could saturate NVMe and iSCSI. Mitigation: stagger pre-warming, use rolling prefetch with backoff, and prefer delta patches for model updates.

Next steps:
1) If you can share preferred maintenance windows we’ll draft a concrete runbook for pre-warm and rollout (attached draft).
2) We need short answers from your ops team on:
   - whether nightly outbound to a cloud bucket is acceptable for backups,
   - if modifying MTU or adding a light storage switch is an option in Q4.

I copied Laura and Neha to iron out the ops-runbook and any encryption/KMS constraints.

— Markus
Director, Private Deployments | Redwood Inference

Team — forwarding Nebula Health thread. Key asks captured below; I want your quick takes on the runbook items and any hard blockers we should flag to the customer. Please reply inline.

Customer constraints: single rack, 3 GPU hosts (4xA100 each), 2x2TB NVMe per host, 24TB NAS via iSCSI, MTU 1500, no new hardware before Q1. Wants minimal ops burden and durable model artifacts.

My suggested mitigations (from my reply):
- 3 control-plane instances on same hardware (non-schedulable for heavy pods)
- Mixed role on host-3 to run storage-gateway + operator daemon for cache prune
- Use local PVs for cache; NAS via iSCSI for canonical artifacts (access through storage-gateway pods)
- Blkio throttling + kubelet eviction tuning
- Nightly encrypted backups to customer-approved cloud bucket

Questions for you:
1) Laura — Can we harden the storage-gateway pattern so we avoid running a full MinIO cluster? Your previous lightweight pattern with read-only gateway + periodic sync looked promising. Any ops caveats?
2) Neha — From a security/compliance angle: is nightly encrypted upload acceptable or do we need an on-prem immutable backup as well? If cloud uploads are allowed, what KMS flow do you want?
3) Jonas — Networking: any concerns with leaving everything on MTU 1500 and using large model transfers over iSCSI during pre-warm? Also any preference for conntrack tuning vs. adding a small L2 jumbo-capable switch (customer says not an option yet).

I’ll collect replies and send a short checklist to Evan.

— Marku(s) (cc: Evan)

Quick answers inline to your questions.

1) Storage-gateway hardening: yes — run a single replica MinIO in gateway mode pointing at the iSCSI backend, but with the following guardrails:
   - Mount the iSCSI volume read-only for the MinIO gateway (MinIO will treat NAS as canonical object store); write operations (model upload) go to a staging directory that the gateway reconciler moves during a maintenance window.
   - Keep a lightweight sync job that snapshots model artifacts (tar + lz4) to a local NAS path, keep last 7 versions, and push encrypted copies to cloud during the nightly window.
   - Use our operator to annotate large model objects so pre-warm jobs can use range requests and staged parallelism rather than a single massive transfer.
   Ops caveats: ensure iSCSI multipath is off (single path to avoid confusing topology-aware provisioners) and set node-level soft/hard eviction thresholds to reserve at least 15% NVMe capacity for system daemons.

2) Neha — Security: if Nebula approves outbound encrypted copies to a cloud bucket, that suffices for our durability SLAs; prefer customer-managed KMS (we can integrate via our KeyWrap flow). If customer requires all backups remain on-prem, we’ll need at least one small spare host for immutable backups (WORM) — otherwise document the operational risk.

3) Jonas — Net: staying at MTU 1500 is fine. For large pre-warm transfers we should:
   - rate-limit transfers and pre-warm in waves,
   - tune conntrack: net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max -> 200k, nf_conntrack_tcp_timeout_established -> 1800,
   - enable tcp_moderate_rcvbuf and BBR to reduce tail latency during concurrent downloads.

I’ll take the runbook draft and add the storage-gateway run/rollback steps and the exact kubelet eviction knobs. Markus — I can turn this into a 1-page checklist to send to Evan.

— Laura
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
